userPrompt: Does an EU data subject have the right to erasure of their account data?
responseText:
**Yes.**

Under the **GDPR** (Regulation (EU) 2016/679), every EU data subject has a **right to erasure** (“right to be forgotten”) in Article 17.

### When the right applies
A data subject can demand that a controller erase their personal data without undue delay if **any** of the following grounds exist:

- The personal data is **no longer necessary** in relation to the purposes for which it was collected or otherwise processed.
- The data subject **withdraws consent** (and consent was the sole lawful basis).
- The data subject **objects** to the processing and there are no overriding legitimate grounds (or objects to direct marketing).
- The personal data has been **unlawfully processed**.
- Erasure is required to comply with a **legal obligation** under EU or Member State law.
- The data was collected from a child in the context of an **information society service** (Art. 8).

### Account data specifically
In practice, this means a user can request deletion of their **account and all associated personal data** (profile, posts, messages, logs, backups, etc.) if one of the above conditions is met. Most consumer-facing services treat a valid erasure request as requiring closure and deletion of the account.

### Important limitations (Art. 17(3))
The controller may **refuse** (in whole or in part) if erasure would:
- Interfere with **freedom of expression and information**.
- Prevent compliance with a **legal obligation** to retain the data (e.g. anti-money laundering, tax, accounting, or regulatory record-keeping rules).
- Be contrary to **public interest** in public health, scientific/historical research, or statistics (where erasure would render the purpose impossible).
- Make the establishment, exercise, or defence of **legal claims** impossible.

### Practical notes for EU controllers
- You must respond **without undue delay** and **within one month** (extendable by two further months for complex cases).
- You must also inform recipients to whom the data has been disclosed (Art. 19), unless impossible or disproportionate.
- You cannot charge a fee unless the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive.
- You must delete or irreversibly anonymise the data; simply “deactivating” an account is usually insufficient.

**Bottom line**: Yes, EU data subjects have a strong right to erasure of their account data, subject only to the narrow exceptions listed in Article 17(3) GDPR. A valid request generally requires the controller to delete the account and associated personal data.
